name: Jalanatheeswarar Temple, Thakkolam
deity: Shiva as Jalanatheeswarar, worshipped as an earth linga (Theenda Thirumeni), with the goddess Giriraja Kanyambika (Giriraja Kannikambal)
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Thondai country, the Thiruvooral of the Tevaram (7th century); a Pallava foundation with Chola and later Nayaka additions
dynasty: Pallava foundation, with Chola endowments and Vijayanagara–Nayaka additions
summary: Jalanatheeswarar at Thakkolam is the Thiruvooral of the Tevaram, a Shiva shrine of the Thondai country where the Lord is worshipped as an earth linga and remembered as the master of the waters, set in a town whose history reaches back to a famous tenth-century battle.

sections.history: Thakkolam stands in the old Thondai country, in the valley west of Kanchipuram now within Ranipet district. In the Tevaram the shrine is named Thiruvooral and is counted among the temples sung by the saints, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam; the hymns are attributed to the child-saint Sambandar. The temple's foundation is held to be of the Pallava age, and inscriptions record the patronage of the Pallava king Aparajita and of the Chola Aditya I, with grants of land, gold, and livestock; the Cholas extended it, and the present masonry and its towered gateway belong to the Vijayanagara–Nayaka period, the rajagopuram dated by inscription to 1543 under Sadasiva Raya. The town itself passed into history as the site of the Battle of Thakkolam of 949, in which the Chola prince Rajaditya fell to the Rashtrakutas — but through every turn of that history the shrine of Jalanatheeswarar has remained its enduring heart. Sources differ on the exact founding date, and the temple has in recent years stood in need of restoration.
sections.architecture: The temple is built in the Dravidian manner, entered through a towered gateway; its rajagopuram was raised in 1543 under the Vijayanagara ruler Sadasiva Raya, while the older sanctum carries the Pallava foundation that the Cholas enlarged. Within, Shiva is worshipped as Jalanatheeswarar in the form of an earth linga, honoured as Theenda Thirumeni, the form not touched by hand, and the goddess Giriraja Kanyambika is enshrined in her own prominent sanctum. Reports of the enclosure's size vary, and some of the stonework has suffered with time, but the layout keeps the dignity of an old royal foundation. Specific measurements are given inconsistently in available sources and are best confirmed on site.
sections.legends: The name Jalanatheeswarar is read as the Lord of the waters, and the temple's legend turns on water: it is said that water once sprang here, flowing from the mouth of Nandi and rising from the earth beneath the Lord, so that the sand linga is honoured as a form born of that living spring. The place is also linked to the great sacrifice of Daksha and its undoing by Veerabhadra, and tradition traces the town's name to Daksha's cry in his last moment. Among the devotees remembered as having worshipped here are Kamadhenu the divine cow, Indra, the Moon, Yama, and the seven celestial maidens, the Saptha Kannikas. These are devotional traditions carried by the temple rather than historical record.
sections.festivals: As a living Shiva shrine the temple keeps the monthly Pradosham, the hours sacred to Shiva, with particular care, and special worship is offered at Guru Peyarchi, the transit of Jupiter. Maha Shivaratri and the ordinary round of the Tamil ritual calendar are observed as at every Shiva temple. Detailed schedules are not fully documented in available sources, so confirm festival and procession dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Thakkolam rewards the visitor drawn to old shrines with long history rather than to crowded pilgrim centres. Enter beneath the Nayaka-period gateway, come to Jalanatheeswarar in the sanctum where the Lord is worshipped as an earth linga, and turn to the goddess Giriraja Kanyambika in her shrine. Those interested in the Pallava–Chola past will find the temple's inscriptions and its association with the tenth-century battle close at hand in the surrounding town. The temple has at times stood in need of care, so a quiet, respectful visit and local guidance are advised; the setting is the plain west of Kanchipuram, among the fields and tanks of the old Thondai country.

visit.timings: One visitor guide gives roughly early morning to midday and again from early evening into the night, with a long midday closure; these hours are not widely confirmed, so check locally before travelling, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals, carvings, or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Thakkolam lies in Ranipet district, in the plain west of Kanchipuram and roughly between Arakkonam and Kanchipuram, both of which are the nearest towns with rail and bus links; Chennai is the nearest major airport. Buses and road transport serve the town, and the temple is near its centre.
